summary: Initial discovery focused on model selection for multilingual customer support and logistics planning use-cases. Main concerns: context window sizing, tool-calling for external systems, latency/cost tradeoffs, and security (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Redwood AE/SE recommended a two-phase pilot: hosted pilot for rapid eval, then Dedicated or Private for production depending on cost and residency needs.
topics: context length and long-form context (30k+ tokens)
open model comparisons and quantization tradeoffs
multilingual throughput and translation vs native multilingual models
deployment modes: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
security: SOC2, KMS, SSO/SAML, audit logs
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-05-14 11:00 AM PDT
- Duration: 47 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Patel (Redwood SE), Olivia Park (Head of AI, HarborEdge), Diego Marquez (Platform Eng), Sofia Nguyen (Security), Ethan Cole (PM)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood inference team, mapped to logistics accounts.
[00:18] Olivia Park: Hi, Olivia here. We wanted to run through a few requirements — main things are: very long context for manifests and routing history, multilingual support across EN/ES/FR/PR, and tool-calling into our TMS/WMS.
[00:32] Lucas Patel: Great, Lucas from SE here. we'll dig into latency SLOs and how model choices affect cost. can you share rough QPS and payload sizes?
[00:45] Ethan Cole: Right now it's low QPS -- prototype ~1–3 rps but big payloads. some requests need 20–30k tokens of context (multi-doc manifests + chat history).
[00:59] Diego Marquez: And we expect bursts during peak shifts, like 8-10 rps for short periods.
[01:12] Maya Chen: Ok good. quick clarifying q: are these token counts raw or after compression/embedding?
[01:22] Olivia Park: raw, typical combined document set. we can prefilter, but prefer model to ingest full state for planning.

[01:35] Lucas Patel: Understood. for 30k+ token context we typically look at long-context variants or windowing strategies. there are two levers: model architecture that supports long context natively and system-level prefix caching / KV cache to avoid resending static sections.
[01:50] Diego Marquez: KV cash? you mean KV cache?
[01:54] Lucas Patel: Yeah, sorry, KV cache — bad transcript there. the cache saves key/value attention states between tokens which can avoid re-encoding the same prefix. Redwood's runtime does continuous caching across requests when you use same session IDs.
[02:08] Olivia Park: That sounds promising. how about model choices — we want open models but don't want huge latency or cost. Any recs?
[02:18] Maya Chen: For open models on GPU, we usually compare a few families: Mistral-gen style medium sized, LlamaX variants, and the new long-context variants like Longformer-esque open checkpoints. tradeoffs: native long-context models reduce engineering complexity but may be heavier per-token; quantized LLaMA derivatives can be cheaper but may need memory tuning.
[02:38] Ethan Cole: Is there an easy way to test multiple models? we don't want to swap infra between runs.
[02:44] Lucas Patel: Redwood Hosted lets you flip model variants via the same API. for Dedicated you can pin specific versions and use routing policies to fall back. so you'll be able to A/B without changing client code.
[02:58] Sofia Nguyen: Security: we need KMS integration for keys, full audit logs, and SSO. also data residency — some manifests must stay in eu. what does Redwood offer?
[03:10] Maya Chen: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS (via cloud KMS/HSM), SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit logs. Hosted can be region pinned; for strict residency and VPC peering we recommend Dedicated or Private. we also include SOC 2 type II documentation — we'll send the pack.
[03:29] Olivia Park: Great. we will want encryption at rest AND transit and an exportable audit trail for all calls.

[03:40] Lucas Patel: Back to models: another dimension is translation vs native multilingual models. you can either translate input to English with a small translator model then run a high-quality EN model, or pick a native multilingual model. translation adds latency but sometimes improves cost if your best EN models are optimized.
[04:00] Diego Marquez: We're worried about latency for real-time driver assistance. target p95 latency should be <600ms for summarize-and-route flows; planning jobs can be slower.
[04:12] Lucas Patel: For sub-600ms p95 you typically use smaller quantized models on dedicated GPUs or Hosted low-latency instances. for long context (30k tokens) the latency will inevitably be higher unless you employ prefix caching and partial reruns.
[04:28] Olivia Park: Can Redwood do tool-calling? we need secure triggers to our TMS APIs with role-based auth and to run deterministic actions like route assignment.
[04:39] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood supports tool-calling and structured output. you can call external connectors via secure credentials stored in your environment. for Dedicated/Private we can set up VPC egress with static IPs and mutual TLS.
[04:55] Sofia Nguyen: On mutual TLS and secrets: is there an option to bring your own HSM?
[05:01] Lucas Patel: Yes, BYO HSM is supported for Private and in many Dedicated contracts; Hosted can integrate with customer KMS in some cases. we'll include an HSM/KMS integration note in the security pack.

[05:15] Olivia Park: ok walk me through a piloting path. we want quick proof with real payloads but safe sandboxing.
[05:24] Maya Chen: Typical path: 1) Hosted pilot using a model variant we pick (e.g., quantized LlamaX-XL or Mistral-medium longctx) with sample data, run weekly benchmarks; 2) Evaluate quality and unit cost; 3) If you need VPC + residency or lower latency with committed throughput, move to Dedicated; 4) If you need on-prem or isolated control plane, Private deployment.
[05:46] Ethan Cole: How long for Dedicated provisioning?
[05:50] Lucas Patel: Depends on committed capacity. small Dedicated pool can be provisioned in 2–4 weeks after contract; larger setups and VPC peering take longer.

[06:05] Olivia Park: For the pilot we specifically want: a) run a 30k-token planning workload b) evaluate multilingual accuracy c) test tool-calling into dev TMS with mTLS. can Redwood run benchmarks or do we provide harness?
[06:19] Lucas Patel: We can run the benchmark with you. we'll need sample datasets and a runbook. Redwood provides reference harnesses and container images. we'll coordinate a 60–90 minute benchmark window for throughput/latency & cost telemetry.
[06:33] Diego Marquez: Will the benchmark measure token-level cost breakdown? we need cost per request at different batching settings.
[06:39] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-token cost, per-route breakdowns, and tracing. we'll also output CSVs that you can import to your cost models.

[06:50] Olivia Park: can you describe caching strategies in practice? we have repeated static manifests and then dynamic driver updates.
[06:58] Lucas Patel: Two patterns: prefix caching where static manifest encodings are cached and reused across requests; and sharded cache + batching where we batch similar requests at the runtime to increase GPU throughput. Redwood Optimize can suggest batch sizes and cache TTLs based on observed latencies. note: caching introduces complexity for freshness, so TTLs and invalidation hooks matter.
[07:22] Sofia Nguyen: any PII concerns? some manifests include driver IDs and customer addresses. how does Redwood handle redaction / tokenization?
[07:32] Lucas Patel: You can use pre-processing hooks to redact or pseudonymize. Private deployments let you keep raw data in your VPC; Hosted supports redaction rules and data retention windows. we'll include redaction examples.

[07:48] Ethan Cole: for multilingual, we care about EN/ES/FR/PT and occasional DE. are there recommended models that handle these natively?
[07:58] Lucas Patel: Mistral and some LlamaX-large variants have decent multilingual coverage; dedicated multilingual models like XGen-Multi or some community long-context checkpoints may perform better. it's model-dependent and we should run a small eval set across the languages you care about.
[08:15] Olivia Park: any auto-translate fallback recommendations?
[08:19] Maya Chen: Common approach: use a small fast translation model as preprocessor for non-English inputs when using an English-optimal model; or use a native multilingual model for uniform behavior. tradeoff is latency vs quality.

[08:34] Diego Marquez: ops question: how are model updates handled? we want pinned versions but also safe rollouts.
[08:42] Lucas Patel: Redwood supports model pinning, canary rollouts, A/B routing and automatic fallbacks. Console gives per-version metrics so you can detect regressions early.

[08:58] Olivia Park: security again: audit logs need to map calls to users and sessions. do you support token-level tracing?
[09:06] Maya Chen: Yes, audit logs include request IDs, session mappings and metadata. for Dedicated/Private you can export logs to your SIEM.

[09:18] Sofia Nguyen: we may need to run a security review with your security team. can we get a compliance questionnaire?
[09:24] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll send the security/compliance packet and coordinate a follow-up review.

[09:36] Ethan Cole: licensing / pricing? we have to evaluate unit costs vs expected savings from automation.
[09:42] Maya Chen: We'll share Hosted per-token pricing + Dedicated reserved tiers. Dedicated pricing has a fixed capacity component and a lower per-token compute rate for committed usage.

[09:55] Olivia Park: ok that's helpful. How about function/tool-calling signing — we need signed requests to our TMS so actions can be auditable.
[10:04] Lucas Patel: You can require an approval step: Redwood can emit a suggested action that your orchestrator then signs and executes. or you can allow direct tool-calls with mTLS and request-level RBAC. both patterns are supported.

[10:20] Maya Chen: Any blockers or must-haves that would stop you from piloting?
[10:25] Olivia Park: three: 1) must have SOC2 & KMS integration, 2) ability to run 30k token benchmark and prove p95 latency numbers, 3) data residency for EU manifests.
[10:36] Maya Chen: All reasonable. we can cover SOC2 and KMS in the security pack, run the benchmark, and discuss Dedicated region pinning or Private deployment for strict residency.

[10:50] Diego Marquez: When you said prefix caching, does that require session affinity? how does that work with load balancing?
[10:58] Lucas Patel: Good call. prefix caching uses session IDs or conversation IDs to tie caches; Redwood routing supports sticky sessions when needed, or a more advanced cache sharing layer where encoded prefixes are sharded by hash. we'll include the architecture note in the benchmark doc.

[11:12] Olivia Park: ok last quick question on quantization — do we see quality drop for instruction-following tasks when going to 4-bit?
[11:20] Lucas Patel: It depends on model and task. some models degrade gracefully; others need finetune or mixed-precision. Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles per workload and we usually validate via eval sets.

[11:32] Maya Chen: Sweet. I'll recap next steps.
[11:35] Maya Chen: Action items: send security pack + pricing (Maya), SE to prepare benchmark plan with container images and sample harness (Lucas), HarborEdge to share a 1k-row sample dataset and compliance checklist (Olivia/Sofia). we'll aim to run a benchmark next week in a dedicated 90-min window.
[11:53] Olivia Park: sounds good. thanks all.
[11:56] Ethan Cole: thanks everyone.
[11:58] Sofia Nguyen: bye.
[12:00] End of recording.

Notes about transcript: occasional mis-transcriptions ("KV cash" -> "KV cache", "Sam El" when SAML mentioned), speaker labels include a proxy. References shared: Security pack link (sent later), Benchmark harness repo (redwood.com/benchmarks/harboredge - placeholder), Pricing sheet (redwood.com/pricing/dedicated-pilot - placeholder).
